h1:
Bang Pa-In Palace
Ayutthaya's Summer Palace on the Water
intro: Bang Pa-In Palace sits about 18 km south of the Ayutthaya island, a summer palace that King Rama V rebuilt into a single garden mixing Thai, Chinese, and European architecture. The spot everyone photographs is the Aisawan Thiphya-Art pavilion floating in the middle of a pond. This guide walks you through what's worth seeing, when it opens, how much a ticket costs, how to dress so you actually get in, and the easiest way to reach it.

blocks.html: If you've toured the temples on Ayutthaya island until your eyes have had enough of ruins, Bang Pa-In Palace is a good change of pace. This isn't a crumbling ruin — it's a palace that's still intact, with wide gardens, green lawns, and several buildings in completely different styles standing inside the same walls. Walking around feels like seeing how Siam under King Rama V borrowed and blended art from many nations.

blocks.text: A Quick History — Why This Palace Is Special

blocks.html: Bang Pa-In Palace dates back to the Ayutthaya period, built during the reign of King Prasat Thong. After the fall of Ayutthaya it was abandoned for a long time, until King Rama IV began to revive it and King Rama V commissioned many new throne halls and residences for use as a royal retreat and for receiving foreign guests. Most of the buildings you see today come from that era.

What sets this place apart from other palaces is how it places architecture from different cultures right next to one another: a Thai-style pavilion in the middle of the water, a full Chinese-style mansion, a European neoclassical throne hall, and a tall lighthouse-shaped tower — all in the same garden.

blocks.text: Throne Halls and Buildings You Shouldn't Miss

items.name: Aisawan Thiphya-Art Pavilion
items.blurb: A Thai-style four-gabled pavilion with a tall spired roof, set in the middle of a pond. It's the symbol of the palace and the most popular photo spot, with a statue of King Rama V inside.

items.name: Warophat Phiman Hall
items.blurb: A European neoclassical throne hall used as the audience hall and royal residence, beautifully decorated inside and still used for some royal ceremonies.

items.name: Wehart Chamrun Hall
items.blurb: A two-story Chinese-style mansion donated by a group of Chinese merchants, with carved woodwork and tiles imported entirely from China — one of the most beautiful and complete Chinese mansions in the country.

items.name: Withun Thasana Tower
items.blurb: A tall lighthouse-shaped tower in red and yellow, built to climb for a view over the whole palace. It's a landmark you can spot from far away.

items.name: Uthayan Phumisathian Hall
items.blurb: A Swiss-chalet-style residence that King Rama V favored. The original burned down and was rebuilt, set in a shady garden.

items.name: Queen Sunandha Memorial
items.blurb: A monument to Queen Sunandha Kumariratana and her children, telling the sad story tied to this palace.

blocks.html: Some buildings are open to enter, others can only be viewed from the outside or close at certain times because they're still used for official functions. Which ones are open changes from time to time, so if there's a particular building you really want to enter, ask the staff at the entrance to be sure.

blocks.text: Opening Hours, Tickets, and Getting Around

items: Opening hours — daily 8:00 AM–4:00 PM, with ticket sales until about 3:30 PM. Coming in the morning is more comfortable to walk before the sun gets harsh.
Admission — Thai adults 30 THB · children 20 THB · foreigners 100 THB · monks and novices free (prices may change, so double-check at the entrance).
Electric golf cart — the palace is fairly large, and you can rent a golf cart to drive around the garden, charged by the hour. Handy if you've come as a group or don't want to walk in the heat.
On foot — if you're not in a rush, walking is easy: flat paths with trees for shade. Seeing the whole place on foot takes around 1.5–2 hours.

blocks.title: A tip for photos
blocks.html: The Aisawan Thiphya-Art pavilion on the water photographs best in the morning or late afternoon when the sun is low — the pond reflects the pavilion clearly. Around midday the sun is straight overhead, making it hard to shoot and very hot.

blocks.text: Dress Code — What's Allowed and What Isn't

blocks.html: Bang Pa-In Palace is a royal precinct, and they're genuinely strict about modest dress — if your outfit doesn't pass, you won't get in. Don't worry though: the entrance has sarongs and cover-up shirts to borrow.

items: Women — sleeved top, a skirt covering the knees or long trousers.
Not allowed — sleeveless tops, tank tops, spaghetti straps, shorts, skirts above the knee, tight leggings, and slip-on sandals without a heel strap.
Jeans — fine as long as they aren't torn or ripped.

blocks.title: Straight talk
blocks.html: If you're coming on a day you plan to shoot photos in traditional Thai dress, check with the palace beforehand whether there's a ceremony or any section closed that day — sometimes the palace hosts official events and closes certain buildings without advance notice.

items: Driving — about 60 km from Bangkok, under an hour. There's parking inside the palace, which is the most convenient option if you come as a group.
Train — take the Northern Line to Bang Pa-In station, then a songthaew or motorbike taxi the short way into the palace. It's the budget option and has plenty of atmosphere.
From Ayutthaya town — about 18 km south. You can charter a taxi, take a Grab, or use a local van. It's often paired in one trip with Wat Niwet Thammaprawat across the river.

blocks.html: Wat Niwet Thammaprawat sits across the river, reached by a small cable car. It's a Thai temple built like a European Gothic church, complete with stained glass. If you have time, it's an easy add-on — it's right next door.

faq.q: What are Bang Pa-In Palace's opening hours and ticket prices?
faq.a: It's open daily 8:00 AM–4:00 PM, with ticket sales until about 3:30 PM. Admission is 30 THB for Thai adults, 20 THB for children, and 100 THB for foreigners; monks and novices enter free. Prices may change, so it's best to double-check at the entrance.

faq.q: How should I dress to get into Bang Pa-In Palace?
faq.a: You need modest dress. Men should wear a sleeved shirt and long trousers; women a sleeved top with a knee-length skirt or long trousers. No sleeveless tops, spaghetti straps, shorts, short skirts, or tight leggings. If your outfit doesn't pass, the entrance has sarongs and cover-up shirts to borrow.

faq.q: What is the pavilion in the middle of the water called?
faq.a: It's the Aisawan Thiphya-Art pavilion, a Thai-style four-gabled pavilion with a spired roof, set in the middle of a pond. It's the symbol of Bang Pa-In Palace and the most popular photo spot.

faq.q: Does it take long to walk the whole palace, and do I need to rent a golf cart?
faq.a: The palace is fairly large, and seeing it all takes around 1.5–2 hours. Walking is easy thanks to flat paths and shade trees. If you've come as a group or want to avoid the heat, there are electric golf carts to rent, charged by the hour.

faq.q: How do I get to Bang Pa-In Palace from Bangkok?
faq.a: It's about 60 km from Bangkok, under an hour by car, or you can take the Northern Line train to Bang Pa-In station and catch a ride into the palace. From Ayutthaya town it's about 18 km south, and it's often paired with a visit to Wat Niwet Thammaprawat across the river.
